back: Land degradation in arid, semi-arid and dry sub-humid areas caused by climatic variation and human activities; it is not the spread of an existing desert.
Physical: drought, variable rainfall, wind and water erosion. Human: overgrazing, overcultivation, fuelwood cutting, poor irrigation, population pressure and poverty.
The number of people or livestock an area can support indefinitely without damage to the land.
Build-up of salts in soil after irrigation in a dry climate: evaporation leaves salts, and poor drainage lets the water table and capillary rise bring more to the surface.
Severe droughts occurred in 1968–73 and 1983–85; they caused famine, loss of livestock and migration.
Farmers protect and prune tree shoots growing from stumps and roots in their fields; cheap, widespread in Niger since the 1980s, with more fuelwood, fodder and higher yields.
Planting pits filled with manure and lines of stones along contours that trap water and soil, used in Burkina Faso and revived from the 1980s.
Launched in 2007 by the African Union; now a programme of land restoration across the Sahel; progress slower than planned and funding uneven.
Stocking (%) = number of livestock units ÷ carrying capacity × 100; capacity = area (ha) ÷ hectares needed per livestock unit.
